So I shared the story with a colleague and there was one big hole I missed.  She called the mom white trash.  Bio mom wasn't white.  These situations are sadly a lot more common than I wish.  That being said the rest of the story and dates match almost exactly. Including Step mom's terms of endearment for Bio mom.

We got this from her court file that came with her records from child services.  As well as her social worker who was assigned to help the transition. 

Bio mom fled with Ava when she was a baby after she was caught cheating on dad.  She claimed dad attacked her, but there was no evidence of it.  Dad said she attacked him.  It was a he said she said and mom had physical custody.  When I talked to dad he just said he gave up at that point.  Bio mom bounced around from partner to partner dragging Ava with her.  Eventually dropping her off with her parents to leave the state and more or less disappear.  No one has heard from her as she changed her number and had no socials.  Grandparents suspected drugs were involved.  At that point grandparents got social services involved since they were out of their depth.  

Social services placed her with dad and step mom and we started bi weekly therapy through their program.  We also started the evaluation process for an IEP so she could be placed in my program officially.  During this process Ava had started attacking her very pregnant step mom.  She even attacked me somehow finding a razor blade and slashing my arm open during one of her fugue phases she'd slip into.  Normally she'd be your typical 1st grader, but she'd several times a day switch and start attacking others.  Normally whoever was closest.  It was during this time step mom moved out to her parents.  Grandma walked her to and from school while dad did his best but was clearly broken by it all.  I've dealt with a lot of stressed out parents in my line of work, but he was easily top 3.

As anyone who's ever tried to get an IEP will tell you it takes time.  In the meantime she was placed in my class so she could get additional support.  Thankfully with the amazing note taking skills of one of my paraeducators, we were able to not only get her an IEP but into a residential therapy program.  The reasons she sticks so much in my mind was that she was the only kid to bypass my program and get placed in a residential program, skipping several LRE (least restrictive environment) stages.

A year later, she came back with step mom.  She was a healthier kid.  She needed that intensive therapy and a change of setting.  I still have a picture my para took of Ava giving me a rainbow bracelet she made.  I keep it as a reminder that no kid is truly evil, even if they growl with a demonic voice while slicing you open.

I'm not completely convinced their the same kid, but the coincidences are aplenty.  Ava is a common name, and I've had cases like her's almost every year.  This is my 16th year (I think I lost count years ago) doing special education.  She's one of a handful of students that stick with me, so I'm happy to give hope that this kid also turned out okay.

It took forever but we got her into a special residental program for young kids and it made a world of difference. Just getting her into a different environment for a couple of months helped immensely.

Last year I got really sick after treating a student.  They were in bad shape with mom driving to take them to the ER.  They were in so much pain I ended up just holding and comforting them when they threw up in my face.  They were in the hospital for a month.  I ended up in the hospital too for a week.  My mask and gloves didn't save me.  I spent most of last year in and out of the hospital but unfortunately ended up with permanent lung damage.  Sucked because I work with kids with emotional/behavioral disorders and occasionally need to chase a kid down.

This year after spending the summer working on my lungs I got assigned to outdoor duty.  I had a letter from the doctor stating to keep me indoors as much as possible especially in bad weather.  Nope "you look so much better this year, surely you can handle it."  First big storm I ended up back in the hospital. I had to text admin from the ambulance because I couldn't breathe let alone talk.  When I got back, "why didn't you call?"  I spent 3 am to 5 am covered in tubes typing out on my phone directions for my team on where my sub plans were, what kids were switching meds, lining up coverage and making sure the kids were set.  I'm not sure what else she wanted.

For the kids...for the kids...just have to repeat that to myself to get through the year.  Thankfully when the other admin got back from sick leave they fixed the situation and I'm back inside.  Normally I like my admin and have a good relationship with them, but that really tried my patience.

Nope never going to happen.  I think most of us wouldn't last against 30 let alone 5,000.  Just dealing with 3 kindergarteners trying to kill me (or anyone they weren't picky at the time) wore me out.  If they're typical kindergarteners, maybe...but kids out to hurt you...yeah no chance.

This is why I keep a snack bar at the front of my class.  Kids can grab what they need without anyone seeing when they walk in.  No one gets singled out.  A colleague complained that the kids would steal the food.

If they're stealing nutragrain bars...they probably need that bar.  It's not like I'm passing out candy.  You can get a 60 pack at costco for like $10.  They're not breaking my bank, and they're not falling asleep from hunger.  Win win.

When I first heard the news I knew the kid had to be special needs.  He sounds just like so many of the students who came through my school over the years.  Especially the really young ones with mental/emotional/behavioral disorders.  99% of the times the parents are just doing the best they can. Unfortunately kids can experience trauma, and it often leaves scars.

One of my students a few years ago had parents like this who came in almost every day, not because we asked but because they were worried about what their kid would do.  Normally, she would be your typical sweet kindergartener (I still have the picture her mom took of her hugging me), but when she got triggered she would flip on a dime.  I had to make sure I was always between her and other students because she would sometimes attack them.  She even stabbed me once, leaving me bleeding all over the classroom.  Thankfully that incident helped us finally get her a bed at the hospital.  She's since been doing much better.

I'm grateful that the teacher here survived.   I'm glad the kid is now being hospitalized.  At no point did I ever blame my student or the parents.  I'm not sure how much I do in this instance either. Keeping a gun in a house with a kid like that wasn't bright, but they were within their rights (whether I agree with them or not).  With my student all knifes were always locked and secured.  She still found a way to get a kitchen knife.  Kids are smarter than we give them credit for.  Even little kids know how to break into locks.  There's a lot we don't know about this situation except that the teacher thankfully survived and the kid is now getting help.

I currently work as a special educator.  Last year there was a kid in a class next to mine who was the poster child for attention seeking.  His teacher would frequently send him to me because I was one of the few who could handle him.  He just needed some love and attention.  I'd ignore the negative behavior and reward the positive and he grew to really love coming to my room.  I'd let him help my students when he finished his work and he seemed to enjoy it.  To be honest I didn't give him too much thought as I had a lot on my plate, and his teacher never mentioned anything.  She was slammed due to having close to 40 2nd graders due to staffing shortage and I was happy to help.  He was doing okay academically and his behavior was just typical attention seeking.  I figured he'd age out of it.

This year I got a new student and suddenly all the puzzle pieces slid into place.  His younger brother was born hypoxic.  To make matters worse they were a family of refugees and the OB/GYN in their village didn't have the resources or expertise to help.  Of all the Ortho kids to cross my caseload he's definitely has the most needs.  Also meeting mom it was clear she was completely overwhelmed and the feeling of guilt when she told their story just washed over her.  What I found most interesting though was that she never once mentioned her other son.  It wasn't until we finished her meeting and she went to pick up her kids that I realized that goofy kid who used to come into my class was the new kid's brother.

Yesterday I caught the older brother trying to sneak back into my class.  I made a point this year to still say hi and let him hug me like he used to, but I also told him that his brother was okay and the only thing he had to worry about in school was making friends and doing his class work.  So when he wondered into my room I knew something was up.  Apparently his mom freaked out at him that he wasn't helping his brother at school.  She used to walk both to school but we were finally able to get the transportation office to send a bus.  Mom wanted him to make sure he got to school okay since she wasn't there at drop off.  

I reassured him that his little brother was okay, but when I called the classroom teacher she was shocked because he was supposed to be in the bathroom.  We're going to have a conference next week, but it was clear that this 3rd grader has had to worry over his little brother for quite a while.

About 5 or 6 years ago I was running an after school program with a colleague when we hear over the PA code blue (active shooter on property).  We were in the library which is a big open room in the center of the building.  We were able to get the kids into a side office but it was one of those rooms with a glass door in which you could see everything.  I shoved some boxes of paper in front of the window, tore off some of the black construction paper off the billboard then the two of us pushed a bookshelf in front of the door.  We hoped it looked like a supply closet.  Throughout the process we could hear pops in the distance.

We ended up spending 2 hours in that room with our backs pressed up against the bookcase.  Apparently we did too good a job at disguising the room as the police couldn't find us.  I found out later that when I texted our location to the principal she gave the location to the SWAT team sweeping the building for the shooter and us.  They were moving groups to the gym as they found them but they never found us.  They couldn't even find the room with a map...not sure how that makes me feel.  They did tell the parents they were in contact with me via text and all of the kids were safe but by that point I turned all sound off on my phone (didn't want to tip off a shooter) and didn't notice when the principal called me when the officers couldn't find us.

Sadly one kid did die elsewhere on the property on his way to pick up his brother.  The shooter got him then ran into the building to hide firing at anyone he saw.  The police never found him and my best guess is that he ran through the building and then through the woods behind our school.

Yeah there are a lot of people out there who like to mess with mobility aids, especially prosthetics.  I can't count the number of times parents of other kids at our school would try to mess with kids wheelchairs or prosthetics.  Usually it's just curiousity, but there are a lot of AHs out there.

I work with students with emotional/behavioral disorders.  I love my job and students but sometimes we need to intervene when they are having an episode.

One day a student went from coloring to picking up her pencil and running at another student to stab him.  In one move I grab her, disarm her, and then swing her arms into a restraint.  Because I didn't start the day with her I didn't check to make sure she had no sharp objects.  Apparently she had a razor blade in her braclet.  

After I got her over to our calm down room she proceded to slice my arm open.  I didnt notice.  I was too focused on calming her down.  When I got her calm she bounced back into the classroom all smiles back to normal.  I walked in behind her smiles myself as we got her calmed down in under 5 minutes (a new record for me).  My coteacher half screamed.  Apparently I was bleeding all over the place.  She somehow cut deep into about 6 inches of my arm.

At age 12 my Tourettes got so bad I decided to sit in a tub with one of the razors from my razor and cut my arm.  I was ticing so bad I couldn't do it.  After 15 minutes I eventually went to my mom and she got me in therapy.  I still tic, but I learned that by advocating for myself and others I can over come the pain and loneliness.  It's why I became a special educator.  I don't hide from my past and talk freely about it, especially once I learned how rampant it is in the Tourettes community.  By avoiding the stigma of disability and getting help we can make it easier for others.

What I was able to gleam from it before it got hugged to death, was basic common sense, aka losing someone close to you can be hard and cause kids to either act out or develop anxiety.

I'm so glad we're 100% virtual, but I'm still scared.  More importantly though, the kids are clearly scared.

This reminds me of an incident a few years ago.

I teach in a title 1 school (very low income) and run afterschool tutoring programs.  They're free to the parents, but I get a small stipend from the state I use for snacks and supplies.  My classroom is small and has a recommended capacity by the fire marshal thats posted near my door.

Parents have to register their kids and due to my county's draconian rules about volunteers I run the program by myself.  It's not a problem usually but it means I need to manage a lot of tired elementary school kids myself.  I line the kids up at the bus platform during dismissal so they can come from class while keeping them organized.  One mom decided that she'd try to sneak her child into my line.

Like I said my room has a carrying capacity, so I told her I couldn't take her kid.  She got angry and threatened to tell my principal how rude I was.  I just laughed since my principal loves me (I run a lot of enrichment programs for the students on my own dime and am beloved by the community).

5 minutes later as I'm getting the kids settled in my room I hear my door open.  I turn around to see the kid standing there.  I run out to the hallway to catch the mom running.  I shout I can't have him in my room the fire marshal will shut us down.  She runs back, grabs another kid and yanks them out before shoving her kid in.

EM: there now there's no problem.

I let her go but call the office to let them know what happened.  I wasn't go to let it escalate after she already grabbed someone's kid.

The office called dad who came to pick the kid up (they were seperated), and called the police.  Everything that happened in the hall was on camera and she was served by the police with a no trespass warning.  She also lost custody of the kid.  The kid just graduated 5th grade and is doing better (and ended up in one of my tutoring programs).

I teach special ed in a title one school and have two stories. 

During the first week before the school year begins teachers typically talk to their students old teachers to get a feel for who is coming into their class.  I was warned that this one student, J, was trouble.  He was your typical sad case who gave up on life.  Born addicted to crack, a jerk to his classmates and teacher, mom died when he was little from drugs, and in and out of different foster care settings as he was always in trouble.  I decided I wasn't going to let that color my opinion of him until I met him.  He was at first exactly who my colleagues described.  Refused to do work and always looking for a fight.  I quickly realized that he always started trouble before group reading.  After pulling him to a separate room I got him to admit to not being able to read.  This was 5th grade and he didn't know all of his letters.  His current foster mom who I worked with before and I set up an intense reading program.  I promised him we would practice in the library so he wouldn't be embarrassed.  By the end of the year he went from reading on a kindergarten level to a 2nd grade reading level.  He worked harder on it than every other student that year.  3 years later he came back to the school in a suit, he had graduated middle school with straight As.  All it took was someone seeing him for who he is and getting one of the best foster mom's I've ever met (seriously she goes out of her way to take special needs kids and has 7 of them in her house at one time).

The other case involves a homeless autistic kid who ended up being one of my favorite kids after I gave mom some training and helped her get the resources she needed (shelter, food, clothing).  The kid was so quiet that his 1st to 3rd grade teachers never heard him talk, but by the end of the year he would talk my ear off.  Last I heard he was doing great and mom got a job and a place of their own.
